periods.activity_title: What Are We Measuring? Activating Metre Sense

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the picture; put a tick mark if length, height, weight, depth, breadth, or temperature is being measured.
What is being used to measure height? What other tools can be used?
Recall Grade 3 learning; check and fill blanks — are the given classroom length statements correct or incorrect?

time_bands.activity: Open with the classroom scene from the book. Children look at the picture and discuss quietly with a partner: what is being measured in each instance? Teacher takes a few responses before moving to Let Us Observe Q1, p.80 ("Look at the picture; put a tick mark if length, height, weight...."), where children mark their answers individually.

Let Us Observe Q2, p.80 ("What is being used to measure height? What other tools...."). Children share their tools list; teacher charts the responses on the board, grouping tools by what they measure, and invites the class to see which tools belong to length.

Let Us Observe Q3, p.80 ("Recall Grade 3 learning; check and fill blanks...."). Teacher reads each classroom length statement aloud; children decide whether it is more than, less than, or exactly a metre. Pairs discuss before writing. Teacher brings the class together for a quick show of answers, correcting misconceptions.

Whole-class closing share: children name one thing in the room they believe is exactly about one metre and one thing much less than a metre. Teacher notes two or three examples on the board to anchor the body-scale intuition built in this unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse the attribute being measured with the tool — they may say 'we measure with a ruler' without connecting the ruler to a length attribute. When children disagree about a classroom statement in Q3, press them to say how they know, not just what they think. No materials beyond the textbook and the board are needed for this unit.

periods.activity_title: Body-Scale Metre: Walk, Jump, Crawl, and Measure

tasks_in_class.description: Draw 1 m, 5 m, and 10 m lines on the floor; walk, jump, and crawl on the lines.
Long jump competition: estimate then measure each student's jump distance using rope combinations; fill the table.

homework.description: Estimate how long and broad the classroom is; measure and check.

time_bands.activity: Teacher and children together cut or pre-mark a 1 m, ½ m, and ¼ m rope piece from string. Children hold the 1 m rope outstretched to feel its length against their arm span and height. Teacher calls attention to how the rope's length compares to a child's height.

Let Us Do Q1, p.81 ("Draw 1 m, 5 m, and 10 m lines on the floor; walk, jump, and crawl...."). Tape or chalk is used to mark the three lines in the corridor or classroom. Children walk, jump, and crawl along each line in small rotating groups while the class observes.

Let Us Do Q2, p.82 ("Long jump competition: estimate then measure each student's jump distance using rope combinations; fill the table."). Each child jumps once; a partner estimates the distance by eye, then the pair uses rope pieces to measure and records both values. The class fills the table together.

Brief wrap-up: teacher asks which was greater — the estimate or the actual jump — for most children, and why estimating is tricky without a physical reference. Homework: Let Us Do Q3, p.82 ("Estimate how long and broad the classroom is; measure and check.").

periods.teacher_notes: Children commonly under-estimate 5 m and 10 m distances because they are comparing to their own height rather than to a laid-out 1 m unit. Encourage children to use the rope piece as a repeated-unit tool rather than guessing in one glance. Ensure enough open floor space and supervise the jumping activity for safety.
materials: Ball of string or thick rope (enough to make 1 m, ½ m, ¼ m pieces per group)
Chalk or masking tape to mark floor lines

section_titles: Estimating Lengths of Animals and Objects
periods.activity_title: Giants and Bats: Reasoning with Reference Lengths

tasks_in_class.description: Answer 5 questions: bus length, bats per whale, buses per two whales, stacked ostriches, crocodiles per whale — using pictured reference lengths.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.83 and examine the animal-length picture. Teacher asks: 'How long is the blue whale shown here? How do you know?' Children share, then the class reads off the labelled lengths — whale ≈ 30 m, crocodile ≈ 6 m, ostrich ≈ 3 m, cricket bat ≈ 1 m. Teacher writes these on the board as a reference panel.

Let Us Think Q1–Q5, p.83 ("Answer 5 questions: bus length, bats per whale, buses per two whales...."). Children work through all five questions individually, writing their reasoning in short. After each question the teacher pauses and invites one child to explain the method — 'How many times does 1 m go into 30 m?' — before moving to the next.

Pairs compare their answers and resolve any differences by re-reading the reference lengths. Teacher facilitates a brief group discussion on Q4 (stacked ostriches) and Q5 (crocodiles per whale), which involve repeated addition rather than simple comparison.
Closing question: teacher names an everyday object (a car, a room) and asks children to estimate its length in metres using the animal benchmarks as a reference. Children share estimates orally.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently confuse 'how many bats fit in the whale' with 'how much longer is the whale than the bat' — they add instead of multiply or divide. Prompt them to use repeated addition first if multiplication is unfamiliar. The animal reference lengths on the board serve as a scaffold throughout the unit.

periods.activity_title: When a Metre Is Too Big: Meeting the Centimetre

tasks_in_class.description: Compare the metre rope with a tailor's measuring tape; observe the marks and discuss how they help measure clearly.
Observe the 1 cm red bar repeated 10 times to make 10 cm; fill: 1/2 m = ___ cm, 1/4 m = ___ cm.

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up a small eraser and asks: 'Can we use the metre rope to measure this?' Class discusses why not. Teacher then displays the tailor's measuring tape alongside the metre rope for Let Us Observe (centimetre section), p.84 ("Compare the metre rope with a tailor's measuring tape; observe the marks...."). Children pass the tape around, count the divisions between 0 and 10, and discuss what each small mark represents.

Teacher draws or shows the red-bar graphic from the book on the board — one 1 cm bar, then the same bar repeated ten times to form 10 cm. Class counts along: '1 cm, 2 cm, … 10 cm.' The key relationship 1 m = 100 cm is stated and written prominently. Let Us Observe (red bar), p.84 ("Observe the 1 cm red bar repeated 10 times; fill: ½ m = ___ cm, ¼ m = ___ cm.") — children reason from the 100-part metre: half of 100 = 50, quarter = 25.

Children work in pairs: one picks any small classroom object, the other estimates its length as 'more than, equal to, or less than 5 cm', then they measure with the tape and record the result in their notebooks. Three pairs share their findings.
Quick oral quiz: teacher calls out a length in metres (3 m, ½ m, ¼ m) and children call back the centimetre equivalent. This consolidates the 1 m = 100 cm relationship through rapid recall.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often read a tape from whichever end they pick up first, giving a reading from a non-zero start without realising it. During the pair activity, circulate to check that children align the zero mark of the tape to one end of the object. Establishing 1 m = 100 cm precisely in this unit underpins all subsequent measurement and conversion work.
materials: Tailor's measuring tape (one per pair or shared)
Small classroom objects for estimation (erasers, pencils)

periods.activity_title: Scale Skills: Measuring Drawn Objects and Small Things

tasks_in_class.description: Measure each drawn object using a scale; write the names in increasing order of length.
Estimate lengths (fingernail, eraser, ant, grain, rajma): equal to, more than, or less than 1 cm; verify by measuring. Write things shorter than 1 cm.
Race three toy cars down a ramp; measure the distance each travels in cm and rank them.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models correct ruler technique on the board: place the zero mark at one end of the object, read where the other end falls. Children open to p.85 for Let Us Do Q1, p.85 ("Measure each drawn object using a scale; write the names in increasing order of length."). They measure each drawn object independently and order the names from shortest to longest.

Let Us Do Q2, p.86 ("Estimate lengths — fingernail, eraser, ant, grain, rajma: equal to, more than, or less than 1 cm; verify by measuring."). Children first write their estimate column without touching a scale, then measure and complete the verified column. Class discusses which estimates were correct and what made 1 cm hard to picture.

Let Us Do Q3, p.86 ("Race three toy cars down a ramp; measure the distance each travels in cm and rank them."). Teacher sets up a simple book-ramp at the front; three volunteers race the cars. The class observes where each car stops; a child marks each stopping point. All children measure the three distances in cm and rank the cars.

Children share their ranked order and the class checks agreement. Teacher asks: 'Did anyone get a different measurement for the same car?' This surfaces the importance of measuring from zero consistently.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error at this stage is reading the ruler from the 1 cm mark instead of the 0 mark, giving every measurement as 1 cm too short. Demonstrate zero-alignment explicitly before Q1 and revisit when children differ on the car distances. The toy-car activity works best with a hardback book or folder as the ramp.
materials: A hardback book or folder to form the ramp

periods.activity_title: Treasure Paths, Hand-Spans, and Broken Scales

tasks_in_class.description: Find the longest and shortest route in a treasure-hunt map (walking on yellow 1 cm tiles); find the length of your route in centimetres.
Trace your hand on paper; measure its length using a scale.
Help Ashwin measure using a broken scale (starting from a non-zero mark); find the two indicated lengths in cm.

homework.description: Use your hand to estimate the measurement of objects; convert into centimetres; verify using a scale. Fill the table.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q4, p.87 ("Find the longest and shortest route in a treasure-hunt map — walking on yellow 1 cm tiles; find the length of your route...."). Children trace each route with their finger, counting 1 cm tiles. They write the total for each route and identify longest and shortest.

Let Us Do Q5, p.88 ("Trace your hand on paper; measure its length using a scale."). Each child traces one hand on a scrap of paper, marks the tip of the longest finger to the base of the wrist, and measures that span with a ruler in cm. Children record their hand length.

Let Us Do Q7, p.88 ("Help Ashwin measure using a broken scale starting from a non-zero mark; find the two indicated lengths in cm."). Teacher shows the broken-scale image on the board and asks: 'If the scale starts at 3 cm, how do we find the real length?' Class reasons: subtract the start value from the end value. Children solve the two measurements.

Quick class check: teacher calls out two start-and-end readings from a hypothetical broken scale and children calculate the length mentally. Homework: Let Us Do Q6, p.88 ("Use your hand to estimate the measurement of objects; convert into centimetres; verify using a scale.").

periods.teacher_notes: Children often count the number of tiles by touching the tile they are on rather than the edge they cross, leading to an off-by-one error on the treasure map. For the broken scale, the key insight is that length = end reading − start reading; children who subtract nothing from the end value are confusing the reading with the length. Ensure each child has paper for tracing their hand.

periods.activity_title: Number Lines, Unit Conversion, and the Sticker Problem

tasks_in_class.description: Fill the blanks on a number line marked in 10 cm intervals (0–100 cm) and in metres (0–1 m); include 25 cm and 33 m.
A board is 2 m long; a decorative sticker is 20 cm long. How many stickers cover the board completely?

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a large number line on the board: 0 to 100 cm in 10 cm steps. Class fills in the values together, then the teacher marks the corresponding metre values below (0 m to 1 m). Let Us Do Q8, p.89 ("Fill the blanks on a number line marked in 10 cm intervals; include 25 cm and 33 m."). Children complete the number-line page individually. Teacher circulates to support those placing 25 cm between the 20 and 30 marks.

Let Us Do Q9, p.89 ("A board is 2 m long; a decorative sticker is 20 cm long. How many stickers cover the board completely?"). Teacher reads the problem aloud and asks: 'Can we use metres and centimetres in the same calculation without converting?' Class discusses the need to convert. Children work individually: 2 m = 200 cm, 200 ÷ 20 = 10 stickers. Three children share their working.

Teacher poses a parallel oral problem: 'A ribbon is 3 m long; each bow needs 25 cm of ribbon. How many bows can be made?' Children think and raise hands. The aim is to check whether children can apply the same two-step (convert then divide) strategy to a new context.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently attempt Q9 by dividing 2 by 20, forgetting to convert metres to centimetres first — the same misconception that surfaces whenever m and cm appear together in a single problem. The number line in Q8 builds the visual support for this conversion, so complete it before moving to Q9. The parallel oral problem at the close confirms transfer without requiring more writing time.

periods.activity_title: Two Ways to Say the Same Length: m and cm Together

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks so well depths are equal: 2 m = 200 cm; __ m = 400 cm; 6 m = __ cm; __ m = 800 cm.
Match wells with the same depth: four pairs of mixed-unit and pure-cm representations.
Measure each student's height using a measuring tape; complete a class table with height in cm and in m.

homework.description: Answer questions: tallest height, shortest height, number of children more than 1 m tall, number shorter than 1 m.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes on the board: '120 cm' and '1 m 20 cm'. Ask: 'Are these the same or different?' Children discuss in pairs. Teacher confirms both are the same length and explains the dual notation using 1 m = 100 cm: 100 + 20 = 120 cm. This motivates the well-depths task.

Let Us Do Q1a, p.90 ("Fill blanks so well depths are equal: 2 m = 200 cm; __ m = 400 cm; 6 m = __ cm; __ m = 800 cm."). Children complete the table individually. Teacher collects answers and demonstrates the pattern: multiply metres by 100, or divide centimetres by 100.
Let Us Do Q1b, p.90 ("Match wells with the same depth: four pairs of mixed-unit and pure-cm representations."). Children draw lines matching the equivalent depths. Pairs compare answers.

Let Us Explore, p.90 ("Measure each student's height using a measuring tape; complete a class table with height in cm and in m."). Groups of four take turns holding the tape against the wall while one child stands against it. One child reads the cm value; the group records it in the class table and then writes the equivalent in m.

Teacher notes the class table is now filled. Homework: Let Us Explore Q1–Q4, p.91 ("Answer questions: tallest height, shortest height, number of children more than 1 m tall, number shorter than 1 m.") — children use the class table they have just helped create.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes write 1 m 20 cm as 120 m instead of 120 cm — the unit label shifts incorrectly when they merge the two parts. Reinforce that the fully-centimetre form drops the metre label entirely. The class-height activity works best with the measuring tape fixed vertically to a flat wall so readings are at eye level.
materials: Measuring tape (one or two per class)

periods.activity_title: Counting the Boundary: Meeting Perimeter Through Bhola's Garden

tasks_in_class.description: Colour the bricks on Bhola's garden boundary; count how many bricks are needed to make the boundary.
Bhola made boundaries in three ways; circle the boundary that is longest.
Find perimeter of shapes on dot grid (1 cm spacing); colour longest boundary blue, shortest green; tick shapes with the same length.

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells the story of Bhola fencing a vegetable garden: 'He wants to put one brick along every edge of the border. How many bricks does he need?' Children open to p.91. Let Us Do (Bhola's garden), p.91 ("Colour the bricks on Bhola's garden boundary; count how many bricks are needed to make the boundary."). Children colour each boundary brick and count. Teacher introduces the word 'perimeter' as the total length of the boundary.

Let Us Do Q1, p.92 ("Bhola made boundaries in three ways; circle the boundary that is longest."). Children examine the three boundary diagrams, count bricks along each, and circle the longest. Class discusses why a shape can have a different-looking boundary but the same or different brick count.

Let Us Do Q2 (a–c), p.92 ("Find perimeter of shapes on dot grid — 1 cm spacing; colour longest boundary blue, shortest green; tick shapes with the same length."). Children count sides along the 1 cm dot grid for each shape, record the perimeter in cm, colour according to the instructions, and tick matching pairs.
Quick oral check: teacher sketches a simple L-shape on the board on a 1 cm grid and asks how many centimetres around its boundary. Children count silently and hold up finger counts.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently count the dots rather than the spaces between them on the dot grid, giving a perimeter one unit too large per side. Demonstrate once that the 1 cm unit is the gap between two dots, not the dot itself. Naming the concept 'perimeter' and returning to it across the unit helps fix the vocabulary early.

periods.activity_title: Equal Perimeters, Real Objects, and Designing Shapes

tasks_in_class.description: Do any of the six shapes (A–F) have the same perimeter? Tick them.
Tick the garden with the minimum perimeter from four options.
Estimate then measure the perimeters of desk, blackboard, classroom floor, and two chosen objects; record estimated and actual values in cm/m.
Draw three different shapes each with a perimeter of 20 cm on a 1 cm dot grid.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q3, p.93 ("Do any of the six shapes A–F have the same perimeter? Tick them.") and Let Us Do Q4, p.93 ("Tick the garden with the minimum perimeter from four options."). Children measure each shape's perimeter on the dot grid and record. After Q3 they compare findings with a partner; after Q4 the class discusses: 'Can different shapes share the same perimeter?'

Let Us Do Q5, p.94 ("Estimate then measure the perimeters of desk, blackboard, classroom floor, and two chosen objects; record estimated and actual values."). Groups of three or four take a measuring tape and move to their assigned object, first writing an estimate, then measuring each side and totalling. Results are brought back and recorded.

Let Us Do Q6, p.94 ("Draw three different shapes each with a perimeter of 20 cm on a 1 cm dot grid."). Children work individually, planning their shapes carefully on the dot grid. Teacher circulates: 'Count the sides before you finish — is the total 20?' Children aim for three visibly different shapes.

Children share one shape from Q6 with the class on the board. Teacher confirms the perimeter count for one example and highlights that very different-looking shapes can share the same perimeter — the core conceptual insight of this unit.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q4 children often choose the largest-looking garden rather than the one with the smallest perimeter, conflating area with perimeter. Prompt: 'We are counting the boundary, not the inside.' For Q5, measuring the classroom floor perimeter is most effective as a full-class activity with the teacher holding one end of the tape. Ensure each group has a tape long enough to span the desk.

section_titles: Estimating Lengths of Animals and Objects
periods.activity_title: Measurement Fair: Connecting Tools, Units, and Boundaries

time_bands.activity: Teacher posts four headings on the board: TOOL, UNIT, ESTIMATE, PERIMETER. Each child writes one example under each heading from any part of the chapter — a tool they used, a unit they measured in, something they estimated, and something whose boundary they found. This activates the full chapter's vocabulary before the synthesis challenges begin.

Challenge 1 — Unit Match. Teacher calls out five lengths (e.g. an ant's body, a classroom door, a blue whale, a jump distance, a well depth) and children choose the best unit (cm or m) and the best tool (ruler, tape, metre rope). Pairs discuss and share; the class arrives at agreed answers. This draws together the tool-and-unit selection thread from the metre-rope work and the centimetre-scale work.

Challenge 2 — Conversion Relay. Teacher writes five conversion blanks on the board (e.g. 3 m = ___ cm; ___ m = 500 cm; 2 m 40 cm = ___ cm; 150 cm = ___ m ___ cm; a 2 m board fitted with 25 cm tiles — how many?). Children solve in notebooks individually, then a volunteer fills each blank. The class checks and corrects, returning to the 1 m = 100 cm relationship and the two-step conversion-then-divide strategy from the sticker problem.

Challenge 3 — Perimeter Gallery. On a fresh dot-grid sheet each child draws two shapes: one with a perimeter of 16 cm and one with a perimeter of 24 cm. They count and label each perimeter. Pairs swap sheets and verify each other's counts. Teacher selects two pairs where both shapes have very different appearances but the same perimeter and shares them with the class, reinforcing that boundary length is independent of shape.

Closing reflection: teacher asks, 'When would you choose a metre rope instead of a ruler? When would you use centimetres instead of metres?' Children give one answer each in a quick round. Teacher summarises: tools match the object, units match the size, and perimeter is always the total boundary — three ideas that run through the whole chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the metre-rope body sense, the 1 m = 100 cm conversion, the broken-scale reasoning, and the equal-perimeter insight — all content already taught. If a class is stronger on one strand than another, spend extra minutes on the conversion relay or the perimeter gallery accordingly. The dot-grid sheet for Challenge 3 must be provided at the start of that band; children should not need to search for materials mid-unit.
materials: 1 cm dot-grid paper (one sheet per child)

items.prompt: Riya jumps and her jump is longer than half a metre rope but shorter than a full metre rope. Write one length in centimetres that her jump could be. How do you know that length fits?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any whole number of centimetres greater than 50 cm and less than 100 cm (for example, 75 cm). The student should state that 50 cm is half a metre and 100 cm is one metre, so the jump falls between them.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the relationship 1 m = 100 cm to find half a metre as 50 cm, then pick a value between 50 and 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student mark 50 and 100 on a number line and point to a value between them; stretch: ask for three different possible jump lengths and explain which is closest to half a metre.

exercise.description: Long jump competition: estimate then measure each student's jump distance using rope combinations; fill the table.

items.prompt: A tailor's measuring tape is more useful than a metre rope for measuring a small ribbon. Which of the following best explains why?

options.label: A
options.text: The tape can only measure things shorter than one metre.

options.label: B
options.text: The tape is divided into centimetres so small lengths can be read precisely.

options.label: C
options.text: The tape is longer than the metre rope.

options.label: D
options.text: The tape is made of a different colour so it is easier to see.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — the tape is divided into centimetres so small lengths can be read precisely.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the graduation of the tape (centimetres) with the plain metre rope to identify the advantage.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses physical length of the tool with its measuring precision — a longer tool is not necessarily a more precise one.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student focuses on a visual feature unrelated to measurement function.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student incorrectly believes the tape has an upper limit shorter than a metre, confusing the scale markings with a physical constraint.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place the tape and rope side by side and point to the small marks; stretch: ask what they would use to measure a room wall and why.

exercise.description: Compare the metre rope with a tailor's measuring tape; observe the marks and discuss how they help measure clearly.

items.prompt: Three toy cars travel down a ramp. Car P travels 18 cm, Car Q travels 23 cm, and Car R travels 14 cm. Write their names in order from the one that travelled the least distance to the one that travelled the greatest distance.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Car R (14 cm), Car P (18 cm), Car Q (23 cm) — from least to greatest.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the three centimetre values directly and arrange them in ascending order.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student mark the three values on a number line and read left to right; stretch: ask how much farther Car Q travelled than Car R.

exercise.description: Race three toy cars down a ramp; measure the distance each travels in cm and rank them.

items.prompt: Diya measures her height as 128 cm. Which of the following shows the same height in metres and centimetres?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 1 m 28 cm, because 1 m = 100 cm and 128 − 100 = 28 cm remaining.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 100 cm (one full metre) from 128 cm to find the remaining centimetres.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student splits the digits 1-2-8 as 12 and 8 without using the 1 m = 100 cm relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student writes 1 m and then copies 128 as 208, showing confusion about what remains after removing one metre.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student treats 100 cm as 2 m, doubling the metre value incorrectly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a number line from 0 to 128 and mark where 100 falls; stretch: ask the student to convert 2 m 35 cm to centimetres.

exercise.description: Measure each student's height using a measuring tape; complete a class table with height in cm and in m.

items.prompt: Colour the boundary bricks of a garden shown on p.91 and count them. The garden is 4 bricks long and 2 bricks wide. Write the total number of boundary bricks needed.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12 boundary bricks. (Top: 4, Bottom: 4, Left side: 2, Right side: 2; total = 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 12.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the bricks along each side of the boundary and add them together.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the grid and trace the boundary with a finger, counting aloud; stretch: ask what happens to the boundary count if the garden is made one brick longer on each side.

exercise.description: Colour the bricks on Bhola's garden boundary; count how many bricks are needed to make the boundary.

items.prompt: Which of the following classroom objects is most likely to be LESS than one metre in length?

options.label: B
options.text: The height of a classroom door

options.label: D
options.text: The length of a new pencil

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — a new pencil, which is typically about 18–19 cm, far less than one metre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each object's known body-scale size against the one-metre benchmark.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not anchored the one-metre benchmark to body scale; a classroom door is typically more than 2 m tall.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not compared the blackboard length to the metre reference; blackboards are typically 2–3 m wide.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses a room dimension with a small object; classroom breadth is many metres.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to stand with arms stretched to show one metre and then hold a pencil alongside; stretch: ask the student to name two more things shorter than one metre and two things longer.

exercise.description: Recall Grade 3 learning; check and fill blanks — are the given classroom length statements correct or incorrect?

items.prompt: Meena estimates the length of her classroom as 7 m. After measuring with a metre rope she finds it is actually 9 m. Was her estimate more than or less than the actual length? By how many metres did she differ?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Her estimate was less than the actual length. She differed by 2 metres (9 − 7 = 2).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the estimate from the actual measurement to find the difference and judge direction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 0 to 10 and mark both values; stretch: ask what fraction of the actual length her estimate was.

exercise.description: Estimate how long and broad the classroom is; measure and check.

items.section_title: Estimating Lengths of Animals and Objects
items.prompt: A blue whale is about 30 m long. A cricket bat is about 1 m long. How many cricket bats placed end to end would equal the length of the blue whale?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the whale's length (30 m) by the bat's length (1 m) to find how many times the bat fits.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to skip-count in 1s from 0 to 30 on a number line; stretch: ask how many bats equal one crocodile (about 6 m).

exercise.description: Answer 5 questions: bus length, bats per whale, buses per two whales, stacked ostriches, crocodiles per whale — using pictured reference lengths.

items.prompt: Priya estimates that a rajma seed is longer than 1 cm. She measures it and finds it is 8 mm (less than 1 cm). What does this tell us about her estimate?

options.label: A
options.text: Her estimate cannot be compared because mm and cm are different.

options.label: C
options.text: Her estimate was more than the actual length.

options.label: D
options.text: Her estimate was the same as the actual length.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — her estimate (more than 1 cm) was greater than the actual length (less than 1 cm), so her estimate was too large.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the estimated value (more than 1 cm) with the measured value (less than 1 cm) to determine which is greater.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not recognise that 'more than 1 cm' and 'less than 1 cm' are contradictory outcomes.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student incorrectly treats the comparison as an equality.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student believes mm and cm cannot be compared, not yet recognising they are both sub-units of the same length scale.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark 1 cm on a ruler and ask the student which side 8 mm falls on; stretch: ask by how many mm the estimate was off.

exercise.description: Estimate lengths (fingernail, eraser, ant, grain, rajma): equal to, more than, or less than 1 cm; verify by measuring. Write things shorter than 1 cm.

items.prompt: A well is 3 m 50 cm deep. Another well is 350 cm deep. Which well is deeper?

options.label: A
options.text: The first well, because it has two separate measurements.

options.label: B
options.text: The first well, because it is measured in metres and centimetres.

options.label: C
options.text: The second well, because 350 is a larger number than 3.

options.label: D
options.text: They are equally deep because 3 m 50 cm = 350 cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — both wells are the same depth. 3 m 50 cm = 300 cm + 50 cm = 350 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 3 m 50 cm to centimetres: 3 × 100 + 50 = 350 cm, matching the second well.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student thinks a mixed-unit notation implies a greater value than a single-unit notation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student compares the digit 350 with the digit 3 without converting units, a classic magnitude-without-unit error.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counts the number of measurements rather than converting and comparing their values.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 3 m 50 cm as ___ cm + 50 cm = ___ cm on a number line; stretch: ask the student to write 4 m 75 cm in centimetres.

exercise.description: Match wells with the same depth: four pairs of mixed-unit and pure-cm representations.

items.prompt: Shape X is a rectangle 5 cm long and 3 cm wide. Shape Y is an L-shape on a 1 cm dot grid with sides of 4 cm, 1 cm, 2 cm, 1 cm, 2 cm, and 2 cm. Do shapes X and Y have the same perimeter? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape X perimeter = 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. Shape Y perimeter = 4 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 12 cm. They do NOT have the same perimeter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add all side lengths of each shape separately and compare the totals.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to trace each shape's boundary with a finger and count each centimetre aloud; stretch: ask the student to redraw Shape Y so that it does have a perimeter of 16 cm.

exercise.description: Do any of the six shapes (A–F) have the same perimeter? Tick them.

items.prompt: A pencil is placed on a ruler. Its left end is at the 0 cm mark and its right end is at the 13 cm mark. How long is the pencil?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 13 cm. The pencil spans from 0 to 13 on the ruler, so its length is 13 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the ruler value at the right end; since the left end is at zero, that value is the length.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 1 to the reading, possibly counting the 0 mark as the first unit.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student subtracted 1 from the reading, likely confusing the number of spaces with the number of marks.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted the start mark from the end mark incorrectly (13 − 0, misread as 1 − 0 after dropping a digit).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show a physical ruler and have the student point to where the pencil ends; stretch: ask the student to measure a second object placed from the 2 cm mark to the 15 cm mark and find its length.

exercise.description: Measure each drawn object using a scale; write the names in increasing order of length.

items.prompt: Look at the number line below. Which value correctly fills the blank marked '...'?
items.visual_stimulus: number_line: 0 cm | 10 cm | 20 cm | ... | 40 cm | 50 cm

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 35 cm. The number line increases in steps of 10 cm; the blank falls between 20 cm and 40 cm at the 30 cm position... wait — re-checking: 0, 10, 20, ___, 40, 50 — the blank is the fourth tick, which is 30 cm. However the verified answer using both routes (count forward: 0+10=10, 10+10=20, 20+10=30; count backward: 50−10=40, 40−10=30) is 30 cm. Correcting: expected answer is 30 cm (option C). NOTE: verification conflict detected — re-running. Forward: step = 10; ticks: 0,10,20,30,40,50 — blank = 30. Backward: 50,40,30 — blank = 30. Both agree: 30 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the step size (10 cm) and count on from 20 cm: 20 + 10 = 30 cm.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student halved the gap between 20 and 40 (finding the midpoint) rather than continuing the 10-step pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added 15 rather than 10, possibly misreading the spacing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student moved forward from 40 instead of backward, placing the blank after 40.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student mark each tick on a blank number line counting in 10s; stretch: ask the student to place 75 cm on a number line from 0 to 100 cm in 10 cm steps.

exercise.description: Fill the blanks on a number line marked in 10 cm intervals (0–100 cm) and in metres (0–1 m); include 25 cm and 33 m.

items.prompt: A rope is 5 m long. How many centimetres long is the rope?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of metres by 100 to convert to centimetres.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write out 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 and add; stretch: convert 7 m 30 cm to centimetres.

exercise.description: Fill blanks so well depths are equal: 2 m = 200 cm; __ m = 400 cm; 6 m = __ cm; __ m = 800 cm.

items.prompt: On a 1 cm dot grid, a rectangle has a length of 6 cm and a width of 3 cm. What is its perimeter in centimetres?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add all four sides: length + width + length + width.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the rectangle on dot paper and ask the student to trace and count each side; stretch: ask the student to find another rectangle with the same perimeter but different dimensions.

exercise.description: Find perimeter of shapes on dot grid (1 cm spacing); colour longest boundary blue, shortest green; tick shapes with the same length.

items.prompt: On a treasure-hunt map, tiles are each 1 cm long. Route A uses 15 tiles and Route B uses 9 tiles. How many centimetres longer is Route A than Route B?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply tile count by 1 cm per tile to get route length in cm, then subtract to find the difference.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw 15 tiles in a row and 9 in another row and count the extra tiles; stretch: ask how many tiles a third route would need to be exactly halfway between the two routes.

exercise.description: Find the longest and shortest route in a treasure-hunt map (walking on yellow 1 cm tiles); find the length of your route in centimetres.

items.prompt: Ashwin's scale is broken at the left end. He places one end of a ribbon at the 4 cm mark and the other end reaches the 19 cm mark. How long is the ribbon in centimetres?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the start reading from the end reading to find the true length.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a ruler segment from 4 to 19 and ask the student to count the gaps; stretch: ask what the ribbon length would be if the scale started at 6 cm and the ribbon ended at 22 cm.

exercise.description: Help Ashwin measure using a broken scale (starting from a non-zero mark); find the two indicated lengths in cm.

items.prompt: A shelf is 3 m long. Each book standing on the shelf is 15 cm wide. How many books can fit on the shelf if they are placed side by side?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 3 m to 300 cm, then divide by 15 cm per book.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a 300-unit line and skip-count in 15s; stretch: ask how many centimetres of shelf space would remain if each book were 18 cm wide instead.

exercise.description: A board is 2 m long; a decorative sticker is 20 cm long. How many stickers cover the board completely?

items.prompt: Draw TWO different shapes on a 1 cm dot grid, each with a perimeter of 12 cm. Label each shape with its perimeter.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two closed shapes whose boundary totals 12 cm each when measured along the 1 cm dot-grid lines. Examples: a 4 cm × 2 cm rectangle (4+2+4+2 = 12), an L-shape with sides 3+1+1+1+2+2 = 10 — no, teacher should verify the student's own shapes by counting. A valid pair: 4 × 2 rectangle and a 3 × 3 square with one corner indented: e.g. sides 3,1,1,1,2,2,1,1 = 12. Teacher counts the student's boundary carefully.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the total boundary length on the dot grid by adding each side; adjust the shape until the total is 12 cm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a 4 × 2 rectangle as a starting example and ask them to find just one more shape; stretch: ask the student to find three shapes with perimeter 12 cm, each with a different number of sides.

exercise.description: Draw three different shapes each with a perimeter of 20 cm on a 1 cm dot grid.
